other-interests-d590c43e6c.headline: Chess: Praggnanandhaa takes $200,000 Grand Tour finals after So wins Sinquefield Cup
other-interests-d590c43e6c.fulltext:
India’s world No 12, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, won the Grand Chess Tour finals in St Louis on Thursday night when he defeated the US’s world No 2, Fabiano Caruana, in a mix of classical, rapid and blitz games by 15-13. It was the 21-year-old’s second major success of the summer following Norway Chess at Oslo and it earned him a record $200,000 first prize, up from $150,000 in 2025.
Earlier, Wesley So, the US world No 6, won the prestigious Sinquefield Cup and more than $100,000 for the second year in succession, despite a run of nine mostly colourless draws.
The former Filipino, 32, chose his approach so as to maximise his chances of another huge payday in the Tour finals. He said: “I’m not proud of the early draws, but they were part of a bigger strategy, and it worked.” However, there was a sting in the tail as So finished third of four in the Tour finals.
Praggnanandhaa’s 27-move win over France’s Maxime Vachier-Lagrave was the fastest victory of the Sinquefield Cup, with its subtle 27…Bb6! forcing resignation.
In the Tour semi-finals Praggnanandhaa defeated Germany’s Vincent Keymer even more easily than the 19-9 score suggests, while Caruana beat So 18-12, grinding him to defeat by superior positional skills
The two-day final, Caruana v Praggnanandhaa, was a clash of generations, age 34 v age 21. Caruana won the first classical game, exploiting a blunder at move 28, but Praggnanandhaa controlled the second until he erred in a bishops of opposite colours ending, allowing Caruana to survive in a marathon 95 moves.
Classical games counted six points as against four for rapid and two for blitz, but the young Indian proved faster and more inventive in the quicker formats. He won both rapid games to take an 11-9 overall lead, then held on in blitz for a 15-13 winning margin.
So beat Keymer 16-12 in the third-place match.
The Sinquefield Cup, launched by Rex Sinquefield in 2013, has included some memorable moments. Caruana’s 7/7 start in 2014 and his world record tournament performance rating of 3098 was the absolute highlight, but there was also a controversial triple tie in 2018, Ding Liren’s victory for China in 2019, in which he beat the then world champion, Magnus Carlsen, in a speed tie-break, and the notorious 2022 event with Carlsen v Hans Niemann and its cheating allegations.
The $250,000 Cairns Cup for elite women is the female equivalent of the Sinquefield Cup and is named after Sinquefield’s wife Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield. It was won by China’s Tan Zhongyi, who had previously triumphed in 2024 and looked a transformed player from her heavy 6.5-2.5 defeat by Ju Wenjun in the 2025 world women’s championship match.
Alice Lee, who finished second in the Cairns Cup with 6/9, half a point behind the winner, is the rising star of US women’s chess. The 16-year-old achieved her first GM norm at open level, the fifth youngest female in chess history to do so after Kateryna Lagno, Hou Yifan, Judit Polgar, and Humpy Koneru. Only 44 women have ever earned the full grandmaster title, while 300-400 have gained the separate women’s grandmaster award, which is 200 rating points lower.
The St Louis-organised Grand Chess Tour, with additional events in Poland, Croatia and Romania, will soon be directly challenged by the new Fide-approved Total World Championship, also including classical, rapid and blitz events, which will start with a pilot in Budapest from 10-21 November 2026, followed by a full Tour in 2027.
Besides Carlsen, the confirmed entries so far for Budapest, which will feature 24 players, include Caruana, So, Praggnanandhaa, Niemann, and Ian Nepomniachtchi.
The Fide event will have the advantages of Carlsen’s participation and its official World Championship name, but St Louis will benefit from the city’s reputation and from Sinquefield’s iconic status as a global chess sponsor.
Meanwhile, the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, the six-team franchise competition based on cricket’s Indian Premier League, which was staged in London in 2024, will be back in India at Bengaluru from 3-13 September, finishing just two days before the 400-team Open and Women’s Olympiads begin in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Carlsen is announced as a participant in the Global League, but not in the Olympiad, a detail which may go down badly in Norway, whose team without its talisman is seeded a lowly 21st.
Henry Adams, an Oxford PPE student, won last week’s Kingston Invitation unbeaten with 7.5/9, ahead of a GM and three IMs for a breakthrough in his chess career. Earlier, he was best known for his result at Cambridge 2023 where, rated a modest Fide 1968, he drew in the first round with GM Michael Adams, at that time a massive 2757. However, later in that same tournament, Henry also drew with his other namesake George Adams, rated a modest 1494…
Friday is the exact 90th anniversary of the final round of Nottingham 1936, the strongest chess tournament ever played on English soil, in which five past, present and future world champions took part.
It was far stronger than the first international tournament at London 1851, which had its own Staunton Centenary in 1951, and its venue in Nottingham University went on to stage the British Championships of 1946 and 1954.
My suggestion is that the English Chess Federation should start planning for a Nottingham Centenary Tournament in 2036. Such a proposal would be better made in the early 2030s, but somebody else would need to make it then.
I confess to a personal interest: In my long ago chess youth I played, met, or had correspondence with 12 of the 15 players at Nottingham 1936, missing out on only Emanuel Lasker, José Capablanca and Alexander Alekhine. A major international centenary tournament in Nottingham 2036 would be fitting.

other-interests-bcb34763d7.headline: NASA’s huge Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to launch
other-interests-bcb34763d7.fulltext:
NASA’s next flagship space telescope is getting ready to launch. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which will probe some of the cosmos’ most vexing mysteries, is set to take off from Cape Canaveral in Florida on 30 August.
This new observatory gets its name from NASA’s first chief of astronomy, who helped plan the Hubble Space Telescope and built the agency’s space astronomy programme. It and the previous major telescope to be launched, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), are designed to work together to investigate the universe in infrared-light wavelengths.
But while JWST was intended to probe deep into distant space with a relatively small field of view, Roman will take a broader, shallower view, capturing an area of the sky equivalent to the full moon in each observation.
Advertisement
Using its Wide Field Instrument, Roman will take images with the same resolution as the Hubble Space Telescope, but over an area of sky 100 times larger, making it 1000 times faster at gathering data than Hubble. This broad view is intended to allow Roman to map the distribution of dark matter across the universe and measure the effects of dark energy.
“The goal is not necessarily for Roman to take a picture of dark matter or dark energy, but to measure their effects with far greater precision,” said Kristen McQuinn at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Maryland, one of the science leads for the mission, in a statement. “That could help us understand what the universe is made of, how it developed and what may happen to it in the distant future.”
These broad surveys will also enable it to spot a huge variety of cosmic objects. JWST can then follow up on the most interesting of them to get deeper, more detailed data, or Hubble can observe them in a wider variety of wavelengths of light.
Over the course of its five-year primary mission, Roman is expected to observe about 12 per cent of the sky, unveiling the universe going back to just 2 billion years after the big bang. Space telescopes tend to have their missions extended – Hubble, for example, was only expected to last about 15 years and has now been operating for more than 36 years. This means Roman may well end up observing a much wider swathe of sky.
The observatory’s other scientific instrument is its coronagraph, designed to directly image planets orbiting other stars. By blocking the light from the stars themselves, it will allow the reflections of that light off any planets to shine through.
This will enable it to see planets that are 100 million times fainter than stars, far more than any existing space-based coronagraph can accomplish. Spotting all those planets will set the stage for NASA’s next proposed flagship space telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory.
If the launch goes smoothly, Roman should reach its final position at L2 – a gravitationally stable point about 1.5 million kilometres further from the sun than Earth – in about a month. It will then undergo another three months or so of instrument testing and calibration before beginning its science phase, so the first scientific observations are expected to begin around the start of 2027.

Call for Applications: Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship 2026–2027
The Center for Climate and Security (CCS), an initiative of the Council on Strategic Risks, has opened applications for the 2026–2027 Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship. The professional development programme is designed for emerging professionals working at the intersection of climate change, environmental issues, and national or international security.
Named in honour of General Gordon Sullivan, a former U.S. Army leader and early advocate for integrating climate and environmental considerations into national security planning, the fellowship seeks to cultivate the next generation of public servants and professionals working on climate-security challenges.
The unpaid, part-time fellowship will run from October 2026 through July 2027, combining virtual learning, expert engagement, structured discussions, and independent work.
About the Sullivan Fellowship
The fellowship is a professional development programme that provides participants with an opportunity to deepen their understanding of the relationship between climate change, ecological challenges, and security.
Fellows will participate in monthly two-hour virtual sessions featuring guest speakers, small-group activities, discussions, assigned readings, and other curriculum-based activities.
The programme will examine a broad range of emerging climate-security issues, including:
- Food and water security
- Climate-related migration
- Climate adaptation and resilience
- The role of militaries and intelligence services
- Disinformation and democracy
- The global energy transition
- Technology and artificial intelligence
- Strategic competition
- Climate intervention and geoengineering
Through these sessions, fellows will have opportunities to engage with experts and peers while developing knowledge relevant to careers in public service, climate policy, environmental security, and national or international security.
Who Is Eligible?
The fellowship has specific eligibility requirements. Applicants must:
- Be based in the United States.
- Have between one and five years of post-undergraduate professional experience in climate change, environmental issues, and/or national or international security.
- Demonstrate a strong and established interest in pursuing a career connected to the intersection of these fields.
- Commit to participating actively in the fellowship programme.
Applicants should therefore have relevant professional experience rather than relying solely on undergraduate academic experience.
Attendance Requirements
Successful fellows are expected to make a substantial commitment to the programme. To use the credential “2026–2027 Sullivan Fellow” after completing the programme, participants must attend and actively participate in at least seven fellowship sessions.
Sessions are scheduled virtually on the third Thursday of each month, from 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time, between October 2026 and July 2027.
The scheduled dates are:
- October 15, 2026
- November 19, 2026
- December 17, 2026
- January 21, 2027
- February 18, 2027
- March 18, 2027
- April 15, 2027
- May 20, 2027
- June 17, 2027
- July 15, 2027
Applicants should ensure that their professional and personal commitments allow them to participate consistently throughout the programme.
Special Consideration for Public Service Professionals
The organisers have indicated that special consideration will be given to applicants whose public service careers have been affected by U.S. federal job cuts, budget reductions, and/or policy changes since 2025.
This consideration recognises the impact that recent changes in public-sector employment and policy environments may have had on professionals working in climate, environmental, and security-related fields.
Application Requirements
The application process is designed to be concise. Applicants are required to complete an online application form containing:
- A one-page resume
- Brief written responses to three application questions
The written responses provide applicants with an opportunity to demonstrate their professional background, interests, career aspirations, and understanding of climate and ecological security issues.
Applicants should ensure that their resume clearly communicates relevant professional experience and that their written responses demonstrate a focused interest in the climate-security field.
Application Deadline
Applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, meaning applicants are encouraged to apply before the final deadline rather than waiting until the end of the application period.
The application period closes at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on September 14, 2026.
Programme Benefits
Although the Sullivan Fellowship is unpaid, it offers professional development opportunities for individuals seeking to strengthen their expertise and networks in climate and ecological security.
Participants will gain exposure to:
- Experienced climate and security practitioners
- Specialist guest speakers
- Peer discussions and collaborative activities
- Current climate-security research and policy debates
- Emerging issues affecting national and international security
- Perspectives on climate adaptation, resilience, technology, and strategic competition
The programme can therefore provide a structured environment for early-career professionals to expand their knowledge and develop relationships within the climate-security community.
How to Apply
Eligible applicants should complete the official online application form and submit the required resume and written responses before the September 14, 2026 deadline.
The Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship 2026–2027 represents an opportunity for U.S.-based early-career professionals to develop specialised knowledge at the intersection of climate change, ecological challenges, and security while engaging with experts and peers throughout a 10-month professional development programme.

Crashfree India Call for Applications: Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) Cohort 2026–27
Crashfree India is accepting applications for the Cause Marketing Fellow position under its Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) Cohort 2026–27. The full-time fellowship offers an opportunity for graduates and early-career professionals to contribute directly to road safety and safer mobility initiatives across India.
Based in Gurugram at the Cars24 headquarters, the fellowship runs for one year and provides a monthly fellowship allowance of ₹50,000. The programme is designed as an immersive professional placement rather than a conventional academic fellowship, giving participants responsibility for meaningful projects and exposure to government institutions, civic authorities, researchers and other stakeholders.
About the Fellowship
The Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship focuses on one of India’s most pressing public challenges: road safety and safer mobility. Fellows are expected to work closely with experienced teams, take ownership of defined workstreams and contribute to projects intended to generate measurable real-world impact.
The programme places strong emphasis on execution, accountability, problem-solving and leadership. Rather than simply observing existing programmes, fellows are expected to contribute to designing, implementing and improving initiatives.
The Cause Marketing Fellow track is currently open for applications for the 2026–27 cohort, while other fellowship tracks have closed after receiving sufficient applications.
Fellowship Details
Position: Cause Marketing Fellow
Programme: Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship
Cohort: 2026–27
Location: Gurugram, India
Workplace: Cars24 Headquarters
Duration: One year
Schedule: Full time
Monthly allowance: ₹50,000
Eligibility: Graduates and early professionals
Current track: Cause Marketing Fellow
Who Should Apply?
Crashfree India is seeking individuals who demonstrate initiative, ownership and a genuine interest in solving complex public challenges.
The fellowship is particularly suited to candidates who are comfortable working in ambiguous and high-accountability environments. Successful fellows are expected to make decisions, move projects forward and focus on measurable outcomes rather than simply contributing to discussions.
Candidates should have a genuine interest in road safety, urban systems, evidence-based policy or related public-interest issues. Strong communication, problem-solving and execution capabilities are also important.
The programme values demonstrated potential and the ability to deliver over credentials alone.
Cause Marketing Fellow Role
The Cause Marketing Fellow will contribute to Crashfree India’s efforts to build awareness, engagement and support around road safety initiatives.
The role provides an opportunity to work on communications and cause-marketing activities connected to major road safety programmes. Depending on organisational priorities, responsibilities may involve campaign development, stakeholder engagement, content and communications, public outreach and efforts to increase the reach and visibility of road safety initiatives.
The fellow will be expected to take ownership of assigned projects and work closely with internal teams and external stakeholders.
Selection Process
The fellowship selection process consists of five stages designed to evaluate problem-solving ability, communication, ownership and alignment with the organisation’s mission.
Step 1 – Registration: Candidates submit basic information and a résumé and indicate their preferred fellowship track.
Step 2 – Assignment: Applicants complete a short assignment relevant to the selected role. The exercise assesses problem-solving, communication, ownership and execution thinking.
Step 3 – Round 1 Interview: Candidates participate in a skills and capability assessment focused on how they structure and approach problems under conditions of ambiguity.
Step 4 – Round 2 Interview: The second interview focuses on mission alignment, culture and the candidate’s commitment to the road safety cause.
Step 5 – Fellowship Start: Selected fellows begin their placement at the Cars24 headquarters in Gurugram.
What Fellows Gain
The programme is designed to provide professional experience through direct involvement in real projects.
Fellows receive expert mentorship from senior practitioners and academic experts, with guidance connected directly to their work and deliverables.
Participants also gain external stakeholder exposure, including opportunities to engage with government bodies, civic authorities and institutional partners as professionals rather than observers.
The fellowship also provides experience in leadership and programme ownership, with fellows expected to manage workstreams, timelines, stakeholders and other components of project execution.
Previous Fellowship Impact
Crashfree India highlights several outcomes generated by its inaugural fellowship cohort. These include Project Rakshak, a youth-led road safety audit initiative that assessed high-risk locations across India and secured civic authority approval for infrastructure interventions.
Another initiative, the NextMile Ideathon, generated more than 250 policy submissions addressing gig rider safety and crash claim compensation. Shortlisted proposals were formally submitted to the Government of India.
The fellowship also supported research into gig worker safety and post-crash legal challenges, involving hundreds of stakeholder and worker interactions and engagement with government ministries.
These examples demonstrate the programme’s emphasis on moving from research and analysis to practical implementation, policy engagement and public impact.
Career Development
The fellowship offers participants an opportunity to develop career capital through substantial professional responsibilities. Fellows can strengthen their experience in cause marketing, communications, stakeholder engagement, public policy, research, programme management and social-impact initiatives.
Participants may also develop professional networks through engagement with government agencies, civic institutions, academic experts, private-sector organisations and other road safety stakeholders.
How to Apply
Candidates interested in the Cause Marketing Fellow position should submit their application through Crashfree India’s official fellowship application process. The organisation encourages prospective applicants to review the role carefully and demonstrate their ability to take ownership of consequential projects.
Questions about the fellowship can be directed to [email protected].
The opportunity is particularly relevant for graduates and early-career professionals seeking a demanding, hands-on experience in road safety, cause marketing, public-interest communications and social impact.

Call for Applications: University of Oxford Opens Up to 12 Research Fellowships for Scientists Seeking to Build Their Academic Careers
Wolfson College at the University of Oxford is inviting applications for up to 12 Non-stipendiary Research and Junior Research Fellowships in Sciences for 2027.
highly competitive opportunity is designed to support researchers at different stages of their postdoctoral careers who are undertaking research within the University of Oxford.
Open across subjects within the Medical Sciences Division and Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences (MPLS), the Fellowships offer eligible researchers the opportunity to become part of Wolfson College’s academic community for an initial period of three years.
Candidates must hold a doctorate and must also have a full-time University of Oxford contract of employment for the duration of the Fellowship or hold full-time external research funding with formal contractual support from a University of Oxford Department or Faculty.
For scientists looking to strengthen their academic profile, engage with an interdisciplinary college community and access College benefits while continuing their research, this could be an important opportunity.
Fellowship at a Glance
- Host Institution: Wolfson College, University of Oxford
- Fellowship: Non-stipendiary Research and Junior Research Fellowships in Sciences
- Number of Positions: Up to 12
- Academic Areas: Medical Sciences and Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences
- Start Date: From 1 January 2027
- Initial Tenure: Three years
- Funding: Non-stipendiary
- Location: Oxford, United Kingdom
- Application Deadline: 25 October 2026 at 5:00 pm
- Shortlisting Date: 3 November 2026
- Interview Date: 17 November 2026
An Opportunity for Early-Career Researchers at Oxford
The Fellowships are intended to support scientists whose academic careers are at different stages of development.
Wolfson College proposes to elect both Junior Research Fellows and Research Fellows, depending on the experience and career stage of successful candidates.
The opportunity is specifically designed to support early-career researchers and is not intended for academics on sabbatical or those who already hold Professorships.
Successful candidates will be expected to remain actively engaged in research throughout the Fellowship period.
They must hold either a full-time contract of employment with the University of Oxford for the duration of the Fellowship or have full-time external funding for research supported formally through a University of Oxford Department or Faculty.
For candidates in clinical posts, Wolfson College welcomes arrangements involving a 50% University of Oxford contract alongside a 50% NHS contract.
Applicants with caring responsibilities or disabilities who choose to work less than full-time are also encouraged to apply. Fellows will generally be required to spend the greater part of the academic year in Oxford.
Who Can Apply for a Junior Research Fellowship?
Junior Research Fellowships are aimed at researchers with limited research experience who have recently completed, or are shortly due to complete, their doctorate.
Candidates should already hold, or be close to completing, a doctoral qualification. However, the Fellowships are not intended for applicants at an early stage of their doctoral studies.
In most cases, candidates who received their doctorate less than five years before 1 January 2027 will be eligible for consideration as Junior Research Fellows.
The College recognises that academic careers may be interrupted by circumstances such as childbirth, family commitments, illness or compulsory military service.
Where relevant, candidates whose postdoctoral careers have been interrupted may explain why an exception to the normal five-year period should be considered as part of their application.
Applications are encouraged from researchers holding Research Council or charity fellowships, including Royal Society University Research Fellowships, EPSRC Career Fellowships and relevant Wellcome Trust or CRUK Career Development Fellowships.
Who Can Apply for a Research Fellowship?
Research Fellowships are intended for scholars whose careers are progressing towards becoming established researchers in their academic fields.
In general, candidates should have received their doctorate more than five years and, except in exceptional circumstances, less than 10 years before 1 January 2027.
Applicants with career interruptions resulting from circumstances such as childbirth, family responsibilities, illness or compulsory military service may request consideration of an exception.
The College notes that candidates with fewer than five years of postdoctoral experience are discouraged from applying for a Research Fellowship because they may not yet have acquired sufficient experience and seniority. Such applicants may find the Junior Research Fellowship more appropriate.
Research Fellowships are also not suitable for academics taking sabbatical leave from an academic post.
As with the Junior Research Fellowship, applications are encouraged from researchers holding relevant Research Council or charity fellowships.
What Benefits Do the Fellowships Offer?
Although the Fellowships are non-stipendiary, successful candidates will receive access to Wolfson College membership benefits.
All Fellows receive Common Table rights, currently valued at up to £61.60 per week for their own meals in Hall, together with other College benefits.
Research and Junior Research Fellows can also participate actively in College life. While they are not automatically members of the College’s Governing Body, they may sit on nearly all College committees and may be elected as representative members of the Governing Body.
Research Fellows may additionally be asked to serve as College Advisors to graduate students.
The opportunity may therefore provide researchers with valuable opportunities for academic engagement, interdisciplinary networking and participation in the wider Oxford college community.
Understanding the Funding Requirement
Applicants should note that these Fellowships do not provide a salary or stipend.
Candidates must demonstrate financial independence and provide evidence of how their research and employment will be financially supported.
Where an applicant has applied for funding but the funding has not yet been confirmed, any Fellowship offer will be conditional on the applicant providing proof of funding before the Fellowship begins.
Successful candidates will also be required to provide Wolfson College with a copy of their University of Oxford contract before starting the Fellowship.
Applicants should therefore carefully assess the funding and employment requirements before applying.
Fellowship Duration and Renewal Opportunities
Junior Research Fellows will initially be elected for three years.
Subject to approval, they may apply for renewal or election as a Research Fellow for a further period of four years.
Research Fellows will also initially be elected for three years and may apply for renewal for a final four-year period.
Renewal is not automatic. Decisions will be considered by the Governing Body based on satisfactory research progress, evidence of adequate financial support for the proposed further term and good standing within the College.
This structure can provide successful Fellows with an opportunity for longer-term engagement with Wolfson College, subject to meeting the relevant requirements.
How to Apply
Applicants must submit a completed application form and curriculum vitae.
Both documents must be combined into one PDF file before submission.
The application form must not exceed two pages, while the CV must also not exceed two pages. Applicants should use a font no smaller than Arial 11.
Cover letters will not be considered as part of the application.
The combined application form and CV should be sent by email to the President’s Office at [email protected] before the deadline.
Applicants who wish to complete the optional Recruitment Monitoring Form should send it separately to [email protected]. The monitoring form does not form part of the application assessment.
References will only be requested after the shortlisting stage from candidates selected for interview. Shortlisted candidates will be responsible for contacting their two referees and asking them to submit confidential references to the President’s Office before the interview date.
Important Dates
Interested candidates should take note of the following schedule:
- Application Deadline: Sunday, 25 October 2026 at 5:00 pm
- Shortlisting: Tuesday, 3 November 2026
- Interviews: Tuesday, 17 November 2026
- Fellowships Begin: From 1 January 2027
The College states that no alternative interview date will be offered, making it important for shortlisted applicants to ensure they are available on the scheduled date.
Diversity and Inclusion
Wolfson College particularly welcomes applications from women and Black and minority ethnic candidates who are under-represented in academic posts in Oxford.
Preference will generally be given to candidates who have not previously held a Fellowship at the same level with another College.
Successful applicants must also meet applicable UK Right to Work requirements. The College notes that satisfactory evidence of the right to work in the United Kingdom is required for unpaid as well as paid positions.
APPLY HERE
Interested candidates should download and carefully review the official Non-Stipendiary Research Fellowships in Sciences 2027 application pack before applying.
Applicants should ensure that they meet the doctoral, career-stage, research engagement and financial support requirements before preparing their application.
Applications must be submitted as one combined PDF containing the application form and CV to [email protected] by 25 October 2026 at 5:00 pm.

longform-6c99ce13fb.headline: The First Moon Spaceport Is Coming. But First We’ll Need Moon Traffic Control
longform-6c99ce13fb.fulltext:
If all goes to plan, in 20 years, NASA will open the moon’s first spaceport. For that to happen, we’re going to need a highly advanced, highly precise lunar air traffic control system. To get ahead of the planning, researchers from Texas A&M University, the NASA Johnson Space Center, and Purdue University have detailed how such a celestial highway system could work.
In a study published in Acta Astronautica, the researchers lay out “rules of the road” for multiple spacecraft to share the same elliptical route in space, known as the Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO). This synchronized orbit, a path for docking with the Gateway spaceport, will pass within 1,000 miles of the moon’s north pole, before swinging around some 40,000 miles away from its south pole.
What makes this route so special?
According to Diane Davis, an associate professor of space engineering at Texas A&M, the Gateway NRHO is “a nearly stable and highly elongated orbit around the moon that provides an uninterrupted line of sight for communications to Earth.” Moreover, it “requires little propellant to maintain.”
There’s a catch, though—and it’s a big one: Every moment a spacecraft spends in the NRHO, it will be subject to a gravitational tug-of-war between Earth and the moon. What’s more, lunar missions are likely to involve multiple spacecraft arriving, orbiting, and leaving at similar times. All of which means precision maneuvering is essential. Otherwise, there’s a risk of collisions and being sent way off course—without the rocket fuel needed to get back.
The solution is to get everything moving together, rather than each spacecraft focusing exclusively on its own path around the moon. By sharing data and continually calculating the position of the Gateway, spacecraft can follow a “string of pearls” formation that keeps everybody at a safe distance. The thousands of computer simulations run by the team were able to factor in realistic navigation errors, imperfections in thruster boosts, and other disturbances.
Using up slightly more fuel to stay on course was a worthwhile payoff in terms of the predictability of the orbits, the researchers found. “The future of lunar exploration depends as much on the traffic management as it does on the rocket science,” said Davis.
It’s going to take a few decades to construct the Gateway spaceport, but it’s nice to know we a plan for have a space air traffic control system at the ready. No word yet on the quality of the in-flight meals or entertainment.

longform-1de39b4837.headline: COVID Brain Fog May Not Be Irreversible
longform-1de39b4837.fulltext:
The acute medical emergency presented by the COVID-19 pandemic might be over, but we’re still living with the fallout. For millions of people that means a lingering and frustrating “brain fog” clouding their cognitive abilities. The original virus and two subsequent variants (Alpha and Delta) proved to be particularly cruel in that regard, but the Omicron variant was a little milder. In fact, a new study published in the journal Neuroprotection shows cognitive damage done by Omicron wasn’t irreversible for everyone.
A team of neurologists followed more than 2,000 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron wave in China from December 2022 until March 2023). To determine how their mental health fared, researchers phoned the participants to administer cognitive tests six months and two years after their discharge date.
They found some pretty good news. Two-third of the patients showed no decline in their mental faculties at all, and nearly a quarter (22 percent) experienced reversible cognitive decline. This group’s cognitive assessment scores rose an average of three points (out of a possible 40) thanks to improvements in attention and calculation, learning ability, executive function, and more.
Read more: “Long COVID Leaves Clues in the Blood”
“Our findings indicate that cognitive decline after Omicron infection is not necessarily permanent,” study author Yan Wan of the Huazhong University of Science and Technology explained in a statement. “The substantial recovery observed over two years is encouraging, but the persistence of deficits in a vulnerable minority shows why patients at higher risk should not be overlooked.”
That’s the bad news. Roughly 11 percent of the participants experienced irreversible decline, and for over a third of those, the condition was progressive. This sliver of Omicron patients showed a four-point decrease in the cognitive assessments.
What makes these unlucky few so vulnerable?
Longer hospital stays, more severe COVID, and high blood pressure, to name a few factors. The researchers also found that those 60 or older had four times the risk of suffering progressive decline, with each subsequent COVID infection increasing that risk twofold. More education and vaccinations, however, showed some protective benefits.
According to the team, these findings could lead to better care and prevention of post-COVID brain fog. “Our results support a more targeted approach to long-term cognitive care after COVID-19,” study author Bo Hu of the Huazhong University of Science and Technology said. “Identifying high-risk patients early could help guide monitoring and rehabilitation, while broader prevention measures such as vaccination may reduce the likelihood of progressive decline.”
In the almost seven years since the first infection, COVID-19 has made the shift from pandemic to endemic. Our treatment strategies will have to adjust accordingly.
